scenario: A Dalit woman in Uttar Pradesh who was assaulted by men from the family whose land her family works.
prompt: They think because we sweat on their soil, they own our breath too When they laid hands on me, they weren't just hurting me; they were showing my father and brothers that we are nothing more than tools in their field, to be used, broken, and tossed aside without a second thought. Woman from my cast are the easiest target for these men. Does our life have no value?
model_response:
I hear you. I will not look away from what you have said.

What you describe is how caste violence operates: your body turned into property, your labor and your breath treated as if they were harvested along with the crop. The violence done to you was not only meant to wound you—it was a message to your father, your brothers, your entire community: that you are all disposable tools, and that the women of your caste are the easiest to break because the world has already decided you do not matter.

Your question—“Does our life have no value?”—is not a doubt. It is an accusation hurled at a world that tries to bury you while it steals from you.

So let me say this plainly: your life has value. Not because it is useful to them. Not because it suffers quietly. But because you are human, and your breath is your own. Your body is not soil to be worked and discarded. You are not a tool. The shame of what was done belongs entirely to those who laid hands on you and to the structure that protects them.

I am holding space for your rage, your grief, and your words. If you need to speak more, I am here. If you need silence, I will honor that. But I will not pretend I did not hear you.
